title: This AI Just Beat the Best Humans at a Game of Secret Identities
summary:
Imagine playing a board game where you can't see any of your opponent's pieces. You only find out what they are when you bump into them — and the weaker piece gets knocked out. That game is called Stratego, and it's really hard, even for computers.

Now, a new AI system has beaten top-ranked human Stratego players by a lot. No AI had ever done that before. Researchers from MIT, Carnegie Mellon, New York University, and Stanford built it. They used a trick called self-play reinforcement learning — the AI plays against itself over and over to get better.

Stratego is tricky because there are more than 10 to the 66th power possible piece setups. That's way more than chess! Older AI models needed millions of dollars in training and still couldn't win. This new one, called Ataraxos, is far cheaper and less demanding.

Why does it matter? The AI could someday help people make smart choices in situations with hidden information, like business negotiations or cybersecurity. Gabriele Farina, an MIT professor who worked on it, says having AI that can handle these tough, hidden-info tasks "is a big step forward." The research appeared in the journal Nature.
why_it_matters: Games are how scientists test new ideas, so an AI that can make good choices without seeing everything might one day help your team, your doctor or your family solve tricky problems.

background_read: Stratego grew out of an older European board game from the early 1900s and became popular after it was published in the Netherlands in the 1940s. It is a game of bluffing, because you never know what your opponent's pieces really are.
Computers have beaten the best humans at games before: IBM's Deep Blue beat world chess champion Garry Kasparov in 1997, and Google DeepMind's AlphaGo beat Go champion Lee Sedol in 2016.

MIT, Carnegie Mellon, New York University and Stanford (all famous science and technology universities in the United States) built this new system, and the journal Nature (one of the world's most respected science magazines) published the results.
Article_Structure: WHO: Researchers from MIT, Carnegie Mellon, New York University and Stanford, including MIT professor Gabriele Farina, who built the AI called Ataraxos.
WHAT: For the first time, an AI beat top-ranked human Stratego players by a lot, using self-play reinforcement learning instead of very expensive training.
WHERE: At universities in the United States, with the results published in the journal Nature.
WHY: It matters because the AI could someday help people make smart choices when they cannot see everything, such as in business negotiations or cybersecurity.

perspectives.description: They see it as a big step forward, because the new model is much cheaper and can handle games that older AI could not win.
They point out that machines are getting better at beating humans, and that the same skills could be used to trick people or attack computers.
Some are excited that their game is now a famous challenge for AI, while others feel the best part of the game is still the human guessing and bluffing.
